To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) autoimmune T cells exacerbate neuropathological changes after nerve injury; (2) nerve injury exacerbates the pathogenicity of autoimmune T cells; (3) nerve injury also exacerbates the neurotoxicity of non‐autoimmune T cells; and (4) the neurotoxic effects of non‐autoimmunity T cells are not mediated via a direct cytotoxic mechanism.
autoimmune and non‐central‐nervous‐system antigen T cells exacerbate neuropathological sequelae of nerve injury.
the immune response to nerve injury is potentiated by prior exposure to central nervous system antigens and that this potentiation results in enhanced neuropathology.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunological mechanisms of neurological recovery after nerve injury.
the immunobiology of neurotrauma.
the immunological mechanisms that underlie tissue damage in the injured nervous system and the role of the immune system in promoting tissue repair.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immune system exacerbates neuropathology after nerve injury, irrespective of the antigen used to activate the immune system.
‘the immune system should not be primed in parallel to nerve injury’.
the data show that neuroinflammation exacerbates nerve injury‐induced neuropathology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune response to nerve injury exacerbates the pathological changes caused by nerve injury, and this effect is not antigen specific.
the immune system is not a good friend of the nervous system.
autoimmune and ‘generic’ T cells are detrimental to nerve regeneration and that the immune system should be modulated to enhance rather than exacerbate nerve repair.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it may be unwise to immunize patients after nerve injury, because this could exacerbate neuropathological damage.
it is important to understand the mechanisms of action of a therapeutic agent, including the immune response, before it can be safely used in patients.
immune priming and injury are not mutually exclusive and, when occurring simultaneously, the outcome is exacerbated neuropathology.
